title: The Free-Lunch Guide to Idea Circularity
gist: Holly Cummins argues that technology ideas recur because tradeoffs shift, not because anything is new, and that the current AI hype, the developer-jobs slump and the layoff wave are better explained by venture-capital incentive structures and the end of the zero-interest-rate period than by AI capability. She reframes ecological, financial, technical, epistemic and sleep debt as one thing - a tradeoff with the future - and predicts Jevons Paradox means AI expands rather than eliminates software work.

themes.theme: Idea Circularity as an Architectural Framework

insights.claim: Technology ideas recur not because the industry forgets them but because the surrounding tradeoff tilts when external assumptions change; grid computing was dismissed and then returned as cloud under new economics.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Screen vendor roadmaps for revived-and-rebranded prior art: the winners are usually old ideas whose enabling assumption just flipped, not genuine novelty.
insights.locator: Anybody remember grid?

insights.claim: London's 1858 Great Stink was caused by a prior 'good' architectural decision - banning cesspits and piping sewage into the Thames - which converted distributed stink and disease into centralized stink and disease rather than eliminating the problem.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: A useful diligence lens: when a platform claims to have removed a constraint, check whether it merely relocated it - the relocation usually shows up later as an operating cost.
insights.quote: Near the bridges the feculence rolled up in clouds so dense that they were visible at the surface.
insights.locator: The problem happened because we had this fundamental tradeoff

insights.claim: Git shipped as a decentralized, distributed source-control model but the market rapidly re-centralized around GitHub, showing that users often want a central authority even when the technology removes the need for one.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Recentralization of a decentralized primitive is a repeatable business opportunity - the same pattern is available wherever a protocol has no dominant hosted control point.
insights.locator: Around that same time, Git was introduced

insights.claim: Java's long-standing conventional wisdom that dynamism, reflection and late binding are good was an artifact of on-premise deployment assumptions, and container-based cloud runtimes invalidate it because the classpath no longer changes at runtime.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Ahead-of-time and build-time-decision runtimes are structurally advantaged in cloud Java; frameworks built on heavy reflection carry a permanent efficiency handicap.
insights.locator: What Quarkus did was it challenged what had been

insights.claim: Measured carbon-as-a-function-of-load experiments showed Quarkus on the JVM has both higher throughput and a lower carbon footprint than Spring Boot, with efficiency and greenness moving together rather than trading off.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Runtime efficiency is becoming a purchasable sustainability metric - watch for cloud bill and carbon reporting converging into the same procurement criterion.
insights.locator: We've measured this. We did some experiments

insights.claim: Apple is deliberately not building its own data centers or foundation models, instead licensing models for a fraction of the cost and pushing AI computation onto hardware customers pay for, while rivals commit hundreds of billions to data centers with questionable ROI.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Apple's capex-light AI posture externalizes inference cost to consumers; if data-center ROI disappoints, that asymmetry becomes a large relative margin advantage.
insights.locator: Some companies are going in a different direction

insights.claim: Amazon Prime Video's widely publicized move from microservices back to a monolith with a 90% cost saving says little about which architecture is correct and much about the fact that the promised free lunch had an unadvertised price tag.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Treat architecture-cost case studies as evidence about hidden operating costs of the prior hype cycle, not as a directional signal for tooling vendors.
insights.quote: We were promised a free lunch, and we have now been extremely disappointed by the price tag.
insights.locator: Amazon Prime Video published a blog a few years ago

insights.claim: Hype is not an accidental property of individual technologies but a structural requirement of how the tech industry's business ecosystem currently raises capital.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Model hype intensity as a funding-market variable rather than a technology-maturity variable; it will persist across whatever replaces AI as the headline.
insights.quote: It's not simply that one piece of technology is overhyped, it's that hype is a necessary ingredient of the current business ecosystem of the tech industry.
insights.locator: Meredith Whittaker, the president of Signal

insights.claim: What actually attracts venture investment is growth and excitement rather than stability, profitability or good management, because each investor needs everyone else to feel the same excitement to enable follow-on rounds and an eventual exit.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Founder and executive claims are optimized for the next round, not for accuracy - discount forward-looking capability statements accordingly.
insights.locator: What attracts investment is growth

insights.claim: The parent company of Cloud Foundry suffered a large stock nosedive when investors discovered it did not contain Kubernetes, a fact obvious to practitioners, demonstrating that public-market pricing tracks buzzword presence rather than architecture.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Buzzword mismatch between a vendor's stack and the current cycle is a repricing risk independent of product quality - and a mispricing opportunity in reverse.
insights.locator: the parent company of Cloud Foundry had this enormous nosedive

insights.claim: Senior AI-vendor predictions have already failed on their own timelines - the claim that AI would write 90% of code within three to six months was made a year earlier - yet similar claims about all white-collar work being automated within eighteen months continue to be issued.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Vendor automation timelines have a documented miss record; underwriting enterprise AI spend to those timelines is a forecasting error, not a base case.
insights.quote: Anthropic's CEO says that in 3 to 6 months, AI will be writing 90% of the code. Unfortunately, he said that a year ago.
insights.locator: We're getting enormous amounts of hyperbole about AI

insights.claim: Companies selling AI products must lay off their own staff to make their product's promise credible, and companies without AI products announce AI-attributed layoffs out of FOMO, a practice Cummins calls AI washing that disguises otherwise poor news.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: AI-attributed headcount cuts are a weak proxy for real AI productivity; look at revenue trajectory before the cut, as with Block, to find the true cause.
insights.locator: This is called AI washing

insights.claim: Overhiring is an accepted business practice of people-stockpiling used to signal success and attract investment, which works until economic cycles turn and forces the correction now being blamed on AI.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: A large share of the current tech layoff wave is a lagged unwind of investment-driven hiring, meaning it should decay rather than compound as rates normalize.
insights.locator: Another factor behind these layoffs is overhiring

themes.theme: Post-ZIRP Rates as the Real Driver of Developer Employment

insights.claim: The zero interest-rate period that ran from roughly 2010 until three years ago, with rates bumping along near 1%, was the historical outlier rather than the norm, and the sharp rise since forced organizations to change how they are run.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Business models calibrated to sub-1% money are structurally impaired at current rates regardless of their technology story.
insights.locator: we had been in what's known as a ZIRP

insights.claim: When government bonds pay around 4%, capital allocators shift money away from high-risk software equity toward safer instruments, which directly reduces hiring and therefore developer jobs.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Developer headcount is a rate-sensitive derivative of venture funding flows - track policy rates as a leading indicator for dev-tool seat growth.
insights.locator: in a post-ZIRP period, all of a sudden that government bond

insights.claim: The peak in developer vacancies coincided with the period of very low interest rates and the slump coincided with rates rising, while the introduction of generative AI barely registered on the job-figure charts.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: The AI-destroys-dev-jobs narrative is not supported by the timing of the data; positioning against dev-tools demand on that thesis is exposed to a rate-driven rebound.
insights.locator: That big peak wasn't with the introduction of GenAI

insights.claim: The latest data shows developer vacancies rising again while overall hiring remains low, so the recovery in developer demand is specific rather than a general economic upswing.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Divergence between developer job postings and aggregate hiring is a concrete, checkable signal that the software labour cycle is turning first.
insights.locator: developer vacancies are going up again

themes.theme: Jevons Paradox and the Infinite Appetite for Software

insights.claim: Jevons Paradox - efficiency improvements increasing total consumption, as when widening a congested highway simply attracts more cars for the same journey time - is predicted to apply directly to software production under AI.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: If AI lowers the cost of code, expect total code volume and therefore spend on running, securing and observing it to rise - bullish for infrastructure and observability, not bearish.
insights.locator: Jevons Paradox says that efficiency improvements

insights.claim: Every previous abstraction layer increased rather than decreased the number of software developers, and COBOL - marketed as English-language programming that would let domain experts and managers write code - instead created the entirely new profession of application developer.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: The no-developers promise has a 60-year failure record; models forecasting AI-driven headcount collapse are fighting a very consistent historical pattern.
insights.locator: each time we've had a new layer of abstraction

insights.claim: Software demand is effectively unbounded - software to manage the software that writes the software - which is why automation expands the field, unlike genuinely finite-demand professions such as the knocker-up human alarm clock that technology did eliminate.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Use demand elasticity as the test for which roles automation destroys versus expands - finite-demand tasks die, unbounded-demand ones compound.
insights.locator: With software, it's really different

insights.claim: Professions using AI are working three hours more per week than they did before AI, which is Jevons Paradox appearing in labour rather than in compute, and the resulting output has been described as disposable busyware.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: AI adoption is currently intensifying work rather than freeing capacity - a warning for productivity-savings assumptions in enterprise AI business cases.
insights.locator: Professions using AI are working 3 hours more per week

insights.claim: The 1930 Keynes prediction of a 15-hour week failed and the historical UK working-hours dataset shows the peak at 66 hours came during the Industrial Revolution's largest productivity gains, so productivity increases have historically raised hours before society chose to lower them.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Any AI thesis that assumes productivity gains automatically convert into reduced labour input contradicts two centuries of the opposite outcome.
insights.locator: In 1930, Keynes said that by the 21st century

themes.theme: Debt as a Tradeoff with the Future

insights.claim: Ecological, financial, technical, epistemic and sleep debt are all instances of a single concept - a tradeoff with the future - and old ideas return precisely when the terms of that tradeoff shift enough that they no longer look like a tradeoff at all.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: A single lens for spotting inflection points: when an environmental variable moves, the previously-uneconomic option becomes the free lunch worth backing early.
insights.quote: Debt is a tradeoff with the future.
insights.locator: Connecting The Dots: Debt, Tradeoffs, and Circular Ideas

insights.claim: Epistemic debt, a term Cummins attributes to Simon Wardley, is the collapse of competence that occurs when teams ship code they do not understand, and it is the distinctive liability created by AI-assisted development.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Organizations accumulating epistemic debt will need review, verification and comprehension tooling - a spend category that grows with AI code volume.
insights.quote: Epistemic debt is the collapse of competence. It's what happens when you ship code you don't understand.
insights.locator: The reason that we need this is to try and get a handle

insights.claim: Code is a liability rather than an asset even when it is good code, so the AI-driven shift of build-versus-buy decisively toward build-then-discard is accumulating technical debt at unprecedented rate.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Firms measuring AI ROI by lines or PRs produced are booking liabilities as output; the correction shows up later as maintenance and incident cost.
insights.quote: What we've agreed to is vibe now, pay later.
insights.locator: Because code isn't an asset, code is a liability

insights.claim: After several outages Amazon told staff to stop using agents, with a reported week-long agent moratorium and a rule that junior and mid-level developers cannot ship agent-produced code without senior sign-off.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: The first large-scale enterprise rollback of coding agents; watch whether human sign-off gates become the standard enterprise control, capping agent seat expansion.
insights.locator: after several outages, Amazon has now told its staff

themes.theme: Sustainability and the Return of Engineering Discipline

insights.claim: The tech industry is responsible for more carbon than aviation, and data centers alone consume as much electricity as a medium-sized country such as the UK.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Data-center electricity demand is now a country-scale load, which makes power availability - not chips - a credible constraint on AI buildout.
insights.locator: The major thing affecting our home is carbon

insights.claim: Low-carbon energy cannot be the whole solution because zero-carbon generation still carries large environmental cost, illustrated by the Itaipu Dam's landscape impact and the Three Gorges Dam moving enough water to lengthen the day by 0.06 microseconds and tilt the earth's axis by two centimetres.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Demand reduction, not just clean supply, will have to feature in credible tech decarbonization stories - relevant to how green-energy-offset AI claims are scrutinized.
insights.locator: even green energy, even zero carbon energy is not without

insights.claim: LightSwitchOps - simply turning systems off when not in use - is blocked not by technology but by learned fear from machines that never worked the same after a restart, so systems must be architected to tolerate being turned off.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Cheap, unexploited cloud-cost reduction: the blocker is restart confidence, which is exactly what resilience tooling and chaos testing vendors sell.
insights.locator: What is LightSwitchOps?

insights.claim: Engineering disciplines that had fallen out of fashion - TDD, small steps, committing as you go, and even written specifications - are becoming fashionable again as a response to AI-generated code that teams do not understand.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Testing, verification and spec tooling is a countercyclical beneficiary of AI code generation rather than a casualty of it.
insights.locator: The Return of Engineering Discipline

insights.claim: The actionable method for spotting recurring opportunities is to ask what problem is being solved, what the tradeoff is, and which assumptions have changed - because changed assumptions are where the payoff sits, as seen in analog computing's energy efficiency, SQL's revival via SQLite, and Quarkus closing Java's performance gap to Go.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: A repeatable screen for early positioning: hunt discarded technologies whose blocking assumption has just been invalidated.
insights.locator: always step back to these fundamental questions

insights.claim: Greenspun's 10th rule, that any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains a bug-ridden implementation of half of Common Lisp, was written by a 29-year-old, showing that pattern recognition about idea circularity is a learnable habit rather than a function of age.
insights.speaker: Holly Cummins
insights.so_what: Historical pattern-matching is a transferable analyst skill, not seniority - it can be taught into a research process.
insights.quote: Any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains an ad hoc, informally-specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of half of common Lisp.
insights.locator: Probably most of you have heard of Greenspun's 10th rule
